{"content": "1|The morning started the way all good mornings in my office started: with Bertha the snake plant judging me from the windowsill and Priya already reorganizing something I hadn't asked her to reorganize.
2|
3|Bertha had been with me since the beginning — a gift from Ira after my first big case, back when I was still figuring out how to be a lawyer and not just someone who owned a law degree. She'd survived my neglect, my erratic watering schedule, and the three weeks I'd forgotten she existed entirely. By now she was four feet tall and had the particular energy of a plant that had decided to thrive out of spite, which I respected. I'd learned, over time, to trust Bertha's opinions on my cases. When a client walked in, she'd tilt toward them if she approved. She didn't tilt for everyone.
4|
5|"Cindy." Priya's voice came through the door before her head did. "The coffee situation is dire. Henry says the bodega on Avenue A changed their supplier and the new beans taste like regret."
6|
7|"Define regret."
8|
9|"Bitter, overroasted, and vaguely disappointed in your life choices."
10|
11|"That's every coffee I've ever had from a courthouse vending machine."
12|
13|"Courthouse vending machines don't charge four dollars for the privilege." She appeared in the doorway holding two paper cups — one black, one with milk — and set them both on my desk with the particular precision of a woman who had strong opinions about beverage temperature. Priya had been my paralegal for almost three years now, and in that time she'd developed a filing system that would make the Library of Congress weep with envy, a label-maker addiction she refused to acknowledge, and an uncanny ability to know what I needed before I knew it myself. She was also the only person I'd ever met who could make the word "okay" sound like a complete performance review.
14|
15|"The milk one is yours," she said. "I took the liberty of assuming you haven't eaten breakfast, because you never eat breakfast, and I brought you a bagel from the place on St. Mark's that you claim is acceptable."
16|
17|"Acceptable is the highest praise I give."
18|
19|"I know. That's why I'm still working here."
20|
21|I took a sip of the coffee. It was terrible. Priya was right. But it was hot, and it was caffeinated, and it was the first thing I'd put in my mouth that morning besides toothpaste, so I drank it with the grateful resignation of a woman who'd learned to take her victories where she found them.
22|
23|The office was small. A desk, a filing cabinet, a bookshelf, a window that looked out onto Avenue A and the particular cross-section of humanity that the Lower East Side offered at nine in the morning: dog walkers and delivery drivers and the man who sold artisanal pickles from a cart on the corner. Bertha had the windowsill. I had the chair. The arrangement had worked for three years and showed no signs of changing.
24|
25|Henry buzzed at nine-fifteen. Henry was my building's doorman — a retired firefighter from Staten Island with the build of someone who'd spent thirty years carrying people out of burning buildings and the temperament of someone who'd decided that the rest of his life would be quiet, or else. He'd adopted me sometime around my second year in the building, when I'd come home at midnight after a case went sideways and he'd simply nodded and said, "Rough one?" and I'd said, "You have no idea," and he'd said, "I was on the job for thirty years. I got ideas." After that, we had an understanding.
26|
27|"Lady here to see you," Henry said through the intercom. "Says her name's Abigail Scott. Says Emily Phillips sent her. Says she's got a story that starts with a dead aunt and ends with a rent-controlled apartment."
28|
29|"Send her up," I said.
30|
31|"Also she's carrying a tote bag that looks like it's been through a war. Just so you're prepared."
32|
33|I hung up the intercom and looked at Priya. "Emily Phillips sent her."
34|
35|"That's the second Emily referral this month."
36|
37|"Third, if you count the one who called about the landlord issue in Bushwick."
38|
39|"The Emily network is expanding."
40|
41|"Mrs. Emily Phillips said you were the one to talk to," Abigail Scott announced from my doorway. She was exactly as Henry had described: a woman in her early sixties with a canvas tote bag that had clearly seen things, a cardigan so aggressively oversized it could have doubled as a tent, and the particular cheerful energy of someone who was about to tell you a very long story and was genuinely excited about it. Her hair was the color of unpainted fence posts and had been styled by what I could only assume was a wind tunnel. She had lipstick on her teeth and reading glasses on a chain around her neck.
42|
43|"She said you saved her boyfriend's life," Abigail continued, settling into the chair across from me without waiting for an invitation. "Or at least his freedom, which she said was basically the same thing, and I thought, well, if she can handle a courthouse theft she can probably handle a family."
44|
45|She said *family* the way most people say *affliction* — with a kind of resigned affection that suggested she'd been thinking about it for far too long.
46|
47|"Tell me about the family," I said.
48|
49|"There are four of us," Abigail said. "I'm the second-eldest, which I'm sure you know means I was the one who did all the actual work while the oldest got the credit and the youngest got away with everything."
50|
51|Her name was Abigail Scott, sixty-one, a nonprofit worker in Midtown who made forty-three thousand dollars a year and had spent the last eleven years taking care of her Aunt Ruth on Sundays. Every Sunday. Not the "I'll call you next week" kind of care, but the real kind — groceries, doctor's appointments, and the particular exhausting labor of loving someone who was slowly disappearing into the accumulated clutter of a life.
52|
53|"Aunt Ruth died three months ago," Abigail said. "She was ninety-two. She'd lived in the same rent-controlled apartment on West 11th Street since 1962. The lease passed to me — she signed it over before she died, proper paperwork, notarized, everything. I have the paperwork. Her lawyer has the paperwork. The building management has the paperwork."
54|
55|"So what's the problem?"
56|
57|"The problem," Abigail said, "is that my brother Derek believes that as the eldest son — he's sixty-three — he has some kind of natural claim to the apartment. The kind of claim that has absolutely no legal basis but a great deal of emotional momentum. My sister Caroline thinks it should go to whoever 'needs it most,' which is a category she has already nominated herself for. And my brother Thomas — who lives in Bushwick in what he calls an 'artist's retreat' and what I call a room with aspirations — thinks there's cash hidden in the walls."
58|
59|"Is there cash in the walls?"
60|
61|"If there is," Abigail said, "it's in Turkish lira. Uncle Max died in 1987 and Ruth spent the next five years buying her groceries at the Turkish place on Bleecker because she thought she was broke."
62|
63|I liked Abigail Scott. I liked her immediately, the way you like someone who tells you the truth without dressing it up first. I liked that she'd shown up with a tote bag that looked like it had survived a natural disaster, that she'd come recommended by a former client who'd called me at seven in the morning two years ago, that she'd already done the hard work of loving someone without expecting anything back.
64|
65|"Let me see the paperwork," I said.
66|
67|Abigail reached into her tote bag and pulled out a manila folder so thick it had its own gravitational field. She set it on my desk with a thud that made Bertha's leaves rustle.
68|
69|"This," she said, "is eleven years of documentation. Eleven years of groceries and doctor's appointments and smoke detector batteries. Plus the original lease, the succession paperwork, and a letter Aunt Ruth wrote to the building manager in 1998 that I found in a box labeled 'Important Correspondence' that also contained three expired coupons and a recipe for meatloaf."
70|
71|I opened the folder. The first document was the lease, dated 1962, signed by Ruth Hartwell and the original building management company. The ink was faded, the paper yellowed at the edges, but the signature was clear — the careful handwriting of a woman who'd understood that she was signing for something more permanent than an apartment.
72|
73|"This is good," I said.
74|
75|"It better be. I spent three weeks going through her boxes."
76|
77|"There are boxes?"
78|
79|Abigail smiled. It was the smile of a woman who had been waiting for someone to ask. "Ms. Walsh, my Aunt Ruth never threw anything away. Not a receipt, not a letter, not a newspaper. Not for sixty years. I have five boxes in my car, and that's just the first load."
80|
81|I looked at Priya, who had appeared in the doorway again, drawn by the word "boxes."
82|
83|"Cindy," Priya said, "I'm going to need you to clarify — are those boxes coming here?"
84|
85|"They're coming here," I said.
86|
87|"The filing system I've built is delicate. It has balance. It has — "
88|
89|"Priya."
90|
91|"I'm just saying. The label maker can only do so much."
92|
93|I turned back to Abigail. "Bring the boxes. I'll look at everything. Give me a week to review the documents and I'll give you an assessment."
94|
95|"A week?"
96|
97|"Six days if you bring the boxes today."
98|
99|Abigail Scott stood up. She extended her hand, and I shook it. Her grip was firm, the grip of someone who'd spent eleven years by a dying woman's side and had no intention of losing the only thing that woman had left her.

The Appellate Division of the Surrogate's Court had ruled on a Tuesday morning in the way that courts rule when they've already decided what they think and the paperwork is just catching up — unanimously, without oral argument, in a three-page decision that said, in the compressed language of appellate conclusions, that the lower court's ruling was affirmed and the lease on the apartment at Hartley House, West 11th Street, apartment 4B, was the legal property of Abigail Scott.

 context line

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute shell commands on a Linux environment. Filesystem usually persists between calls.

Do NOT use cat/head/tail to read files — use read_file instead.
Do NOT use grep/rg/find to search — use search_files instead.
Do NOT use ls to list directories — use search_files(target='files') instead.
Do NOT use sed/awk to edit files — use patch instead.
Do NOT use echo/cat heredoc to create files — use write_file instead.
Reserve terminal for: builds, installs, git, processes, scripts, network, package managers, and anything that needs a shell.

Foreground (default): Commands return INSTANTLY when done, even if the timeout is high. Set timeout=300 for long builds/scripts — you'll still get the result in seconds if it's fast. Prefer foreground for short commands.
Background: Set background=true to get a session_id. Almost always pair with notify_on_complete=true — bg without notify runs SILENTLY and you have no way to learn it finished short of calling process(action='poll') yourself. Two legitimate uses:
  (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers, daemons) — silent is correct, there's no exit to notify on.
  (2) Long-running bounded tasks (tests, builds, deploys, CI pollers, batch jobs) — MUST set notify_on_complete=true. Without it you'll either forget to poll or sit blocked waiting for the user to surface the result.
For servers/watchers, do NOT use shell-level background wrappers (nohup/disown/setsid/trailing '&') in foreground mode. Use background=true so Hermes can track lifecycle and output.
After starting a server, verify readiness with a health check or log signal, then run tests in a separate terminal() call. Avoid blind sleep loops.
Use process(action="poll") for progress checks, process(action="wait") to block until done.
Working directory: Use 'workdir' for per-command cwd.
PTY mode: Set pty=true for interactive CLI tools (Codex, Claude Code, Python REPL).

Do NOT use vim/nano/interactive tools without pty=true — they hang without a pseudo-terminal. Pipe git output to cat if it might page.

command.description: The command to execute on the VM

background.description: Run the command in the background. Almost always pair with notify_on_complete=true — without it, the process runs silently and you'll have no way to learn it finished short of calling process(action='poll') yourself (easy to forget, leading to silent blindness on long jobs). Two legitimate patterns: (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers, daemons) — these stay silent because there's no exit to notify on. (2) Long-running bounded tasks (tests, builds, deploys, CI pollers, batch jobs) — these MUST set notify_on_complete=true. For short commands, prefer foreground with a generous timeout instead.

timeout.description: Max seconds to wait (default: 180, foreground max: 600). Returns INSTANTLY when command finishes — set high for long tasks, you won't wait unnecessarily. Foreground timeout above 600s is rejected; use background=true for longer commands.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command (absolute path). Defaults to the session working directory.

pty.description: Run in pseudo-terminal (PTY) mode for interactive CLI tools like Codex, Claude Code, or Python REPL. Only works with local and SSH backends. Default: false.

notify_on_complete.description: When true (and background=true), you'll be automatically notified exactly once when the process finishes. **This is the right choice for almost every long-running task** — tests, builds, deployments, multi-item batch jobs, anything that takes over a minute and has a defined end. Use this and keep working on other things; the system notifies you on exit. MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE with watch_patterns — when both are set, watch_patterns is dropped.

watch_patterns.description: Strings to watch for in background process output. HARD RATE LIMIT: at most 1 notification per 15 seconds per process — matches arriving inside the cooldown are dropped. After 3 consecutive 15-second windows with dropped matches, watch_patterns is automatically disabled for that process and promoted to notify_on_complete behavior (one notification on exit, no more mid-process spam). USE ONLY for truly rare, one-shot mid-process signals on LONG-LIVED processes that will never exit on their own — e.g. ['Application startup complete'] on a server so you know when to hit its endpoint, or ['migration done'] on a daemon. DO NOT use for: (1) end-of-run markers like 'DONE'/'PASS' — use notify_on_complete instead; (2) error patterns like 'ERROR'/'Traceback' in loops or multi-item batch jobs — they fire on every iteration and you'll hit the strike limit fast; (3) anything you'd ever combine with notify_on_complete.
